## Summary
Two jurisdictions currently have operative, compute-triggered frontier-model obligations: the **EU AI Act** and **California SB 53**. The apparent third jurisdiction—the United States—did adopt a **10²⁶-FLOP** threshold in 2025 policy instruments, but it did **not** leave an operative federal developer-reporting regime: BIS’s proposed reporting rule under Executive Order 14110 was never finalized, EO 14110 was rescinded, and the separate AI Diffusion Framework’s “controlled model” threshold was not a finalized general developer-reporting requirement comparable to the EU and California laws.

| Jurisdiction | Exact threshold | Legal instrument and threshold provision | Obligation triggered | Effective date / current status | Estimated coverage of publicly announced or identifiable training runs |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| **European Union** | **More than 10²⁵ FLOPs** of cumulative training compute | **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Art. 51(2)**. The calculation includes compute used to improve capabilities before market placement, including pre-training, synthetic-data generation, and fine-tuning. | A provider whose general-purpose AI model is presumed to have systemic risk must notify the European Commission **without delay and no later than two weeks** after the condition is met (**Art. 52(1)**). Systemic-risk providers also have evaluation, risk-mitigation, serious-incident reporting, and cybersecurity duties (**Art. 55**). | Chapter V rules on general-purpose AI became applicable **2 August 2025**. The threshold creates a **rebuttable presumption**; the Commission can designate models below it based on capabilities or impact. | **Largest coverage.** An April 2025 estimate identified about **30 publicly available models** trained above 10²⁵ FLOPs. |
| **California** | **More than 10²⁶ integer or floating-point operations** of cumulative training compute, including specified fine-tuning and material modifications | **SB 53, Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act, Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22757.10** (definition of “frontier model”); related disclosure and incident provisions are **§§ 22757.11–.12**. | Developers must publish a transparency report when deploying a new or materially modified frontier model. They must report critical safety incidents to the California Office of Emergency Services—normally within **15 days**, or within **24 hours** where there is an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. Developers and affiliates exceeding **$500 million** in annual gross revenue must also maintain, publish, and annually review a frontier-AI framework. | Signed **29 September 2025**; operative **1 January 2026**. | **Smaller coverage.** The April 2025 estimate identified about **two publicly available models** above 10²⁶ FLOPs. Every such run exceeds the EU’s 10²⁵-FLOP threshold, but many EU-threshold runs do not exceed California’s. |
| **United States (federal)—not an operative reporting regime** | **More than 10²⁶ FLOPs** in the proposed BIS reporting rule; the 2025 AI Diffusion Framework separately used the same level for “controlled models” | **EO 14110 § 4.2** directed BIS to develop a reporting rule; BIS proposed one on **11 September 2024**, **89 Fed. Reg. 73,612**. The later AI Diffusion Framework separately used the 10²⁶-FLOP “controlled model” concept. | The BIS proposal would have required confidential and continuing reports on qualifying training runs and large computing clusters. It was only a proposal; the Diffusion Framework was not a substitute finalized developer-reporting regime. | **No effective reporting date.** BIS never finalized its rule, and EO 14110 was rescinded. Thus this is not comparable to the operative EU and California reporting duties. | Had it taken effect, its numerical reach would have matched California’s: roughly **two** publicly identified models in the April 2025 estimate. |

On a raw compute comparison, the **EU’s >10²⁵-FLOP threshold captures the largest number of currently announced or publicly identifiable runs**, because it is one order of magnitude below California’s—and the non-operative U.S. federal proposal’s—**>10²⁶-FLOP** threshold. The best cited contemporaneous estimate, from April 2025, was approximately **30** publicly available models above 10²⁵ FLOPs versus **2** above 10²⁶ FLOPs.

Those figures are indicators rather than a worldwide legal census. Epoch AI’s underlying database is deliberately non-exhaustive and focuses on models that are publicly documented and “notable” (for example, state-of-the-art, highly cited, historically significant, significantly used, or costly). Its compute estimates may be based on reported training compute, hardware-time and utilization assumptions, or architectural operation counts. For its records, Epoch reports total training compute including pretraining and pretrained base components, while separately recording fine-tuning; legal calculations can instead depend on each statute’s specific treatment of pretraining, fine-tuning, modifications, providers, and market or deployment nexus.

The difference in threshold reach is likely to become more consequential over time. Epoch AI estimates compute for frontier and notable models has grown about **4–5× per year** from 2010 through May 2024. Its May 2025 projection places the median number of notable, publicly announced models with a new training run above **10²⁶ FLOPs** at roughly **10 by 2026**, **30 by the start of 2027**, and **more than 200 by the start of 2030**; alternative scenarios projected roughly 10–80 such models by 2027. A related forecast projected that, by the end of 2028, **103–306** foundation models could exceed **10²⁵ FLOPs**, versus **45–148** exceeding **10²⁶ FLOPs** (90% confidence intervals). These are projections of publicly estimable notable models, not counts of every model legally covered.
